newsitem.title: COTE D'IVOIRE: Zaire's Kabila to send team to OAU summit.
newsitem.headline: Zaire's Kabila to send team to OAU summit.

text.p: Rebel leader Laurent Kabila has been invited to attend Wednesday's special Organisation of African Unity (OAU) summit on Zaire's civil war and has said he will send a delegation, host Togo said on Monday.
Togo's Foreign Ministry said in a statement that both Kabila and his arch-rival, veteran President Mobutu Sese Seko, had been formally invited to take part.
Foreign Minister Pierre Koffi Panou told Reuters that Kabila, whose forces control a fifth of the sprawling Central African nation, had agreed to send a delegation.
"That's a positive sign," Panou said by telephone, adding that Kabila's representatives had not so far taken part in other major meetings on the five-month-old war.

Mobutu, back in Zaire after fresh cancer treatment, has not said whether he will attend in person but his journey home on Friday left him so drained that he sent away an official welcoming committee and did not appear in public until Sunday.
"I'm in the process of examining the question," he told journalists in Kinshasa on Sunday.
Before leaving France for home, Mobutu called for a truce and talks and the creation of a national council to find ways out of the crisis "with all our brothers, without exclusion".
His government has backed a U.N. ceasefire and talks plan but Kabila, his popularity rising with each battlefield victory, says talks must come before any truce.
Kabila repeated his position on Saturday in Zaire's captured third city of Kisangani during talks with U.N. special envoy Mohamed Sahnoun, who has been spearheading peace efforts.
Kabila has called for a transitional government to run Zaire for no more than a year but says he will not work with anyone who has shared power with Mobutu.

The government, he said on Saturday, should include his Alliance for Democratic Forces for the Liberation Congo/Zaire "and only anti-Mobutists and anti-regime people who have never been in power and who never shared power".

Mobutu, 66, has ruled Zaire since seizing power in an army coup in 1965, but many ordinary Zaireans, ground down by three decades of poverty and hardship under his rule, are eager for a change and are openly rallying to Kabila.
Mobutu, appearing in public on Sunday for the first time since his homecoming, took delivery of a letter from South African President Nelson Mandela.
Asked about his plans and whether he would negotiate with Kabila, he replied: "In the next 48 hours you will know."
Mandela's deputy Thabo Mbeki, who delivered the letter, said afterwards that a U.N. peace plan for a truce and talks was at the heart of efforts to end the war.
"We are convinced that in the immediate future steps will be taken practically to move the peace process forward towards a resolution," Mbeki told reporters in Kinshasa.

He said the U.N. Security Council had spelled out "a very important position" in its resolution and he highlighted its call for a truce and negotiations. "I think these are particular matters of focus that everyone is looking at," he added.

The rebels, who took up arms in October over a dispute about nationality for an ethnic Tutsi minority in the east, say their forces are 200 km (125 miles) from Zaire's second city Lubumbashi, capital of the southern mining province of Shaba.
